thinking_and_logic: The submitted implementation does not contain the logic needed to solve Two Sum: it iterates but performs no checks and returns a fixed answer. A correct approach (per the answer key) is either brute force over all pairs (O(n^2)) or the optimal single-pass hash map: for each number x at index i, compute complement = target - x; if complement has been seen, return [seen[complement], i]; otherwise record seen[x] = i. Checking before inserting prevents using the same element twice.
code_assessment: Your final code contrasts sharply with the canonical solution: it does not implement complement lookup (hash map) nor pair enumeration, and it hardcodes the output, which the answer key explicitly calls out as a known pitfall. As a result, it fails basic scenarios where the correct pair is not at indices [0,1] (e.g., "pair at end") and also fails edge cases like negatives and empty input. The optimal approach would pass all tests in O(n) time and handle the full input size constraint (up to 1e5) reliably.
